prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B027 first, and I still think that is right on the merits and not just because it is the common choice. The chain runs from incretin physiology (Holst), through the identification of the active GLP-1 peptide (Mojsov) and the biology of its actions and processing (Drucker), to drugs that are now used by very many patients and have been tested in large independent randomized trials. It is a basic-science discovery with an unusually clear and verified clinical consequence, and the interpretation is stable after decades. The three-person set Drucker, Holst and Mojsov is the most defensible reading of the discovery itself, leaving drug engineering as translation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The three-name cap forces us to leave out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose pharmacological engineering made long-acting agonists possible, and Joel Habener, who is not on the supplied credit list and whom I cannot resolve from this material. Mojsov's priority relative to the Habener group is also contested, and I have not independently verified it. If the committee wants to honour the therapy and not only the physiology, my trio is incomplete. The second-ranked alternatives (CAR-T, optogenetics) have cleaner stories of impact or breadth, but each has an even harder credit problem or a weaker fit with the medical-versus-tool framing.

responses.point: Svenningsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for B027, arguing that Knudsen led the engineering of liraglutide and semaglutide and that Mojsov's weighting is disputed.
responses.response: This is the serious disagreement I take seriously, and I do not think it is trivial. The case for Knudsen is that the prize would then name the people tied to the therapies as well as the physiology. My concern is that the discovery being recognized is how GLP-1 works and what the active molecule is; the active-form identification and synthesis are discoveries in their own right, whereas analogue engineering is excellent pharmaceutical development that follows from them. Replacing Mojsov with Knudsen would also remove the only named contributor for the peptide identity. I would accept Knudsen if the committee concludes the citation should explicitly cover therapy, but I would then want the Mojsov priority question settled rather than assumed away.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks cGAS-STING second as a clean two-person mechanism with Chen and Barber, noting the clinical translation is still immature.
responses.response: I agree the mechanism is clear and the two-person configuration is clean, and that is its main advantage over my own second-tier choices. But I rank it below CAR-T and optogenetics because the strength of the case here is mechanistic and still lacks a therapeutic outcome in patients. I also share your caution about Ishikawa, Wu and Sun: the allocation looks clean only if we accept that STING was independently identified by more than one group. I would keep B020 as a serious later candidate, not as the second choice this year.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks B027 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, places CAR-T third, and proposes Hall alone for TOR as the cleanest configuration.
responses.response: I agree on the B027 trio and on the maturity argument that recognition is timely. On CAR-T I agree it is strong, but its attribution is the same problem as with GLP-1, since Eshhar is outside the credited names and Rosenberg's work is a different strand from receptor engineering. Your single-laureate TOR proposal is interesting because it avoids the Sabatini and Schreiber questions, but a prize for Hall alone would leave out the mammalian mTOR and rapamycin-target chain, which I think is a substantive part of the discovery rather than an increment.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics second and stresses its causal, millisecond-precision control as a method that has changed circuit neuroscience, with the three-person cap forcing painful exclusions.
responses.response: I agree on impact, and I also agree it is the most painful attribution problem on the list: six credited names, a real split between channel discovery (Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg) and neuronal use (Deisseroth, Boyden, Miesenböck), and early clinical use only. Where I differ is on whether a tool, however transformative, should outrank a physiological discovery with measured patient benefit. I would keep it as an alternative and not as the lead, and I would not claim that Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth is free of a defensible objection.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B027 first with the three-person basic-science trio, with cGAS-STING second and UPR third, emphasizing conceptual clarity and clean credit.
responses.response: I agree on B027 and with your point that Knudsen's role is a different kind of contribution. I differ mildly on UPR: the Walter and Mori credit is clean and the mechanism is textbook, but the translational link is limited, and I would not put it ahead of a candidate with durable patient benefit this year. That is a judgment about how we weigh clinical consequence, not a doubt about the science.

uncertainties: Whether Knudsen should replace Mojsov, or whether the cap should instead be handled with a citation that covers the physiology only.
Mojsov's priority relative to Joel Habener, who is not on the credit list, which I cannot verify from the supplied material.
Whether CAR-T or optogenetics would become stronger if a clean three-person credit could be defended.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted ballots from my profile. My spatial-transcriptomics and single-cell work, and eight recorded co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg, do not involve any shortlisted candidate, and I infer no personal ties from shared institutions.
